articles.title: Ema raises $77M as AI starts eating into enterprise software and services | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Ema has raised $140 million to date and has more than 50 enterprise customers, including Google and Microsoft.
articles.body:
Ema , a startup that uses teams of AI agents to automate corporate processes across HR, IT, and finance, has raised $77 million in a new funding round as it aims to take on more of the work traditionally handled by enterprise software and IT services.

The Series B round was led by Bengaluru-based venture firm Creaegis, with existing investors Accel, Section 32, and Prosus increasing their stakes. The financing brings the startup’s total funding to $140 million and more than quadruples its valuation from its last funding round in 2024. (Ema declined to disclose its latest valuation.) The round consisted entirely of primary equity, with no debt or secondary transactions, the startup confirmed to TechCrunch.

The funding comes as AI is beginning to compete for dollars that businesses have traditionally spent on enterprise software and IT services. Startups, major AI labs, and established software companies are now fighting to capture that spending.

Founded in 2023 by former Google and Coinbase executive Surojit Chatterjee and ex-Okta executive Souvik Sen, Ema is looking to expand its position in that market. The startup deploys its technology, which it calls “AI employees” — systems that coordinate multiple AI agents. These help carry out multi-step business processes across a company’s existing applications, rather than handling a single task at a time.

Chatterjee sees that model eventually reducing companies’ reliance on traditional software products, including those sold as software-as-a-service (SaaS). Ema first “wraps” around an enterprise’s existing applications, he said, before customers can reduce their dependence on some of those products — and, in some cases, replace them altogether.

“Many of our customers are already on the way to replace [large SaaS applications] completely, removing dependency on them, because they are mostly becoming like a database,” Chatterjee said.

In recent months, major AI companies have also pushed deeper into the enterprise market where Ema operates. Anthropic has expanded efforts to bring Claude into companies’ core operations, including financial and legal work. Similarly, OpenAI has established teams of forward-deployed engineers who work alongside customers to put AI into production.

Chatterjee, however, does not see the frontier AI labs as direct competitors. He told TechCrunch that Ema’s software can draw on more than 150 models, including frontier and open source models, while the startup focuses on the domain knowledge, integrations, and orchestration needed to automate business processes end-to-end.

“Progress in frontier models is actually very beneficial to us,” Chatterjee stated.

Ema’s approach is already gaining traction. The startup has more than 50 active enterprise deals, as well as over 1 million active enterprise users, and has handled more than 5 million actions and queries. Its customers include NTT DATA, Hitachi, ADP, PwC, Google, KPMG, Wipro, and Microsoft.

Over the past two years, Ema said its revenue has grown 50-fold, while revenue bookings have surpassed $150 million. Chatterjee said the bookings figure includes the total value of multiyear contracts, including two- and three-year deals, rather than representing annual recurring revenue. He, however, declined to disclose the startup’s current annualized revenue run rate.

Chatterjee told TechCrunch that more than 90% of Ema’s customers have expanded beyond their initial use case, with some deploying the technology across dozens of workflows. The startup’s net dollar retention rate is around 180%, he said, meaning existing customers are spending substantially more with Ema over time.

Ema is also looking beyond the software itself. AI, Chatterjee said, can take over some of the implementation, integration, and consulting work that companies have traditionally paid IT services firms to perform around enterprise software.

“A lot of the services companies are working with us,” Chatterjee said. “They are also dramatically changing or disrupting their own business models because they understand the human-forward model may not be the best model going forward.”

Despite taking on work traditionally handled by software and services providers, Chatterjee said Ema has maintained gross margins of close to 80%. The startup, he noted, requires less human support as its AI systems learn from deployments, helping improve margins over time.

Ema also does not charge customers based on software seats or the number of AI tokens they consume. Instead, Chatterjee said, its pricing is tied to the completion of tasks and business outcomes.

Much of Ema’s new capital will go toward expanding its go-to-market operations, particularly sales and marketing, after spending its first years largely building the product, Chatterjee said. The Mountain View-headquartered startup has grown to nearly 200 employees and has its offices in Bengaluru, London, and Vancouver.

Ema has so far focused primarily on customers in the U.S. and Europe. However, it now plans to expand into new markets over the next year, particularly across Asia-Pacific, South America, and parts of the Middle East.

articles.title: Comma's hands-off driving tech under investigation after 2 fatal crashes | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The investigation involves at least some crashes where it appears drivers were using "forked" versions of Comma's software.
articles.body:
Comma.ai , the startup founded by hacker George Hotz, is facing a federal investigation after five reported crashes involving the company’s aftermarket hands-off driver assistance tech, two of which resulted in three deaths.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of Defects Investigation (ODI) said this week that the reported crashes involved Comma.ai devices failing to detect or respond to slow or stopped vehicles in the same road lane. Across four of the crashes, as many as 11 people were injured, some seriously.

Some of the crashes, including at least one of the fatal incidents, may have involved the use of “forked” or modified versions of Comma.ai’s software, according to the ODI.

Comma.ai could not immediately be reached for comment. Hotz, who distanced himself from the startup’s day-to-day operations in 2022, did not immediately return a request for comment.

Founded in 2015, Comma.ai makes devices that can be installed on a range of modern cars. The devices — and Comma.ai’s software, “openpilot” — can control a car’s Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) and Automated Lane Centering (ALC) systems to perform functions “similar to Tesla Autopilot and GM Super Cruise,” according to the startup’s website. The goal is to “make driving chill.”

Comma.ai’s website claims that “openpilot can steer, accelerate, and brake automatically for other vehicles within its lane.” Still, much like Tesla and GM, Comma.ai warns drivers that they “must always be capable to immediately retake manual control of the vehicle, by stepping on either pedal or by pressing the cancel button.” The company’s device uses a camera-based driver-monitoring system to watch for distracted or sleepy drivers.

One of the two fatal crashes appears to have happened in February 2026 in Ascension Parish, Louisiana. A 2022 Toyota RAV4, which was running FrogPilot, a third-party fork of openpilot, struck a stopped first responder vehicle.

Louisiana State Police released details of a crash in February that appear to match the report in the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s database. In that crash, the Toyota struck a “fully marked Gonzales Police Department unit, was unoccupied and positioned in the left lane with emergency lights activated while officers investigated a separate crash.” The state police said two rear-seat passengers of the Toyota died.

The other fatal crash couldn’t be immediately identified by the report numbers cited by the ODI.

Advanced driver assistance systems have historically struggled with stopped or slow vehicles, or other stationary objects. Tesla and Ford have faced similar investigations after their systems were involved in multiple crashes.

Comma.ai’s own website states that the “performance” of openpilot Adaptive Cruise Control can be affected by “vehicles in the same lane that are not moving.”

“When abrupt braking maneuvers are required,” the company writes, “openpilot is designed to be limited in the amount of deceleration and acceleration that it can produce.”

articles.title: PitPro’s first tire-changing robot goes live in Canada
articles.summary: The startup says its automated system can change four tires in under 15 minutes.
articles.body:
If you live in Canada, this year’s set of snow tires might be installed by a robot.

San Francisco startup PitPro Automation said Wednesday that it has installed its first automatic tire-changing system at a tire shop in Calgary, Alberta. The startup says its robotic system, first revealed last year, can swap a full set of four tires in under 15 minutes. The first deployment is at a Kal Tire location — one of Canada’s largest independent tire service chains.

PitPro is one of myriad startups trying to disrupt different parts of the car ownership experience. While founder and CEO Jeremy Conrad told TechCrunch he ultimately wants to move into other kinds of automated maintenance, he thinks there’s big opportunity to build a business around tires in the near term.

Changing tires is “backbreaking” work, and tire shops are facing a major labor shortage, he said in an interview. Even when shops can find people for the job, he said, those workers often leave within a few months to a year.

“One shop manager was telling me they had to get special permission to pay more because a Panda Express opened across the street and it took about half their employees,” he said.

PitPro’s system is designed to slide right into existing maintenance bays. It features two boxy robots, each roughly the size of an oven, that use a mix of sensors and a robotic arm to locate and loosen the lug nuts. The robots store the lug nuts, pull off each the wheel, and replace it with a new or rotated tire.

PitPro has, to date, mostly talked up plans to deploy its tire-changing robots with commercial fleets. It’s still focused on that line of business, Conrad said, and the startup has former Ford Pro executive Ted Cannis as an adviser. (“He’s got relationships with basically kind of every major fleet in the United States, and he’s you know been very helpful in making introductions for us on that,” Conrad said.)

But Conrad believes tire chains are a major opportunity as well, not just because of the labor shortage, but because of the constant demand for tire changes — especially in Canada, where switching to and from winter tires is a yearly occurrence for most car owners.

Conrad said PitPro is focused on chains, rather than smaller shops, since they tend to have standardized layouts and offer greater potential for wider deployment down the road. On top of that, mechanics can still use the bay that PitPro’s tech occupies for other maintenance, increasing the chance that shops will be willing to try it out, Conrad said.

The shift to real-world deployment has had its challenges, according to Conrad. Tire shops tend to operate with the bay doors open, which exposes PitPro’s robots to all kinds of dust, debris, and weather. The startup had to account for all that, not only to keep the system robust, but also to make sure the sensors maintain an accurate view of the tires.

Not everything is a challenge, though. During the interview, Conrad shared a photo from the Calgary installation showing where the robots had been almost completely covered in an unexpected substance: dandelion seeds.

“We looked into it, and it’s not going to be a problem for us,” Conrad laughed. “But it’s just like… I had never thought about that we might need to deal with a dust cloud of dandelions.”

articles.title: Spotify's is giving you the keys to its recommendation algorithm with US launch of 'Taste Profile' | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Spotify is rolling out Taste Profile to Premium users in the U.S., letting listeners see how the streamer understands their tastes and use natural language to reshape their recommendations
articles.body:
Spotify is giving listeners a new tool to shape the recommendations it delivers to their app’s Home feed.

The music streaming giant on Wednesday began rolling out a feature called “Taste Profile” to its Premium subscribers in the U.S. that allows users to see, for the first time, how Spotify understands their taste across music and other audio. Users can request changes using natural language commands to fine-tune their recommendations, or make broader changes.

Powered by Spotify’s AI, Taste Profile was first unveiled in March at the SXSW conference in Austin by Spotify co-CEO Gustav Söderström. However, the feature was initially available in beta only to listeners based in New Zealand.

Now, the feature is arriving in Spotify’s largest market in terms of traffic and revenue, where it will be put to a larger test among listeners ages 18 and up.

In some ways, Taste Profile essentially gives you the keys to Spotify’s algorithm. It is how the streaming platform chooses what music and podcasts to suggest, including in its flagship Discover Weekly playlist, its Made for You recommendations, and the highly anticipated annual review known as Spotify Wrapped.

Though Spotify’s algorithmic understanding of a listener’s habits is largely credited as the secret to its success, those recommendations don’t always reflect users’ evolving tastes. The platform often ends up recommending too-similar music when a user would rather branch out.

Now, by editing their Taste Profile directly, Spotify users can request more variety or ask for more or less of a certain genre, artist, or overall vibe.

The feature could be used to remove recommendations based on music that users may regularly stream, but not necessarily care to see more of — for instance, sleep sounds played at night, or whatever music a teenager plays while in the car on their parent’s account.

Until now, Spotify has offered some options to remove music from your Taste Profile, but they only let you exclude certain tracks or playlists . More recently, the company added a much-requested toggle switch that would prevent kids’ music from impacting their parents’ recommendations.

To access Taste Profiles on the mobile app, first tap on your profile pic, then scroll down and select Taste Profile. From here, you’ll be able to explore how Spotify currently understands your taste across music, podcasts, and audiobooks. Under “Tell us more,” you’ll then enter what you’d like to adjust and send the message.

After a few hours, your app’s Home Page will reflect a different set of suggestions.

Spotify says the feature can be used when you want to explore a new genre or era, but aren’t sure where to start, or if you want to adjust the vibe of the music — like if you want more energizing tracks. You can also tell Spotify what sort of podcasts and audiobook you want to better shape those recommendations.

The feature is still in beta. The company didn’t offer a timeline as to when it would reach a wider audience.

articles.title: YouTube adds new creator tools like video A/B testing, dynamic thumbnails, and live dubbing | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Many of these tools hinge on using generative AI to try out a variety of different tactics on a video to find what works best.
articles.body:
In a bid to help creators reach more people, YouTube on Wednesday unveiled a slew of new tools, many of which use AI to try out different tactics on videos to find what makes them perform best.

The new Ask Studio feature allows creators to share draft videos with AI to get personalized feedback based on their previous content and user comments. The feature will propose alternative titles and thumbnail options, analyze the creator’s channel analytics to explain the performance of their videos, and offer advice for improving metrics. Ask Studio is expanding to YouTube’s mobile apps, too.

YouTube already allows creators to A/B test titles and thumbnails, and from 2027, this feature will let creators upload and test three different cuts for Shorts. There’s also a Dynamic Thumbnails feature, with which creators can upload multiple thumbnails and leave it to YouTube to determine which thumbnail to show viewers that is most likely to spark their interest.

Creators can also apply these tools to their existing catalog. If a creator allows it, Ask Studio will be able to autonomously monitor thumbnail performance and create tests to refine older videos.

On the shopping front, YouTube will now use AI to auto-tag products, which it says will help creators earn money through affiliate programs. The company is also expanding its Amazon affiliate program beyond the U.S.

Some creators are understandably skeptical of using AI to support their content, worrying that just one AI-generated mistake could harm their credibility. For such features to succeed, they will need to be accurate enough to assuage creators’ concerns.

The platform is also giving creators new ways to go live. Early next year, YouTube will pilot auto-dubbing on live videos to translate creators’ speech into other languages in real time. The company is also launching a “live showdown” feature, which lets creators co-host streams together, and even get paired with other creators currently streaming through “live creator matchmaking.”

“Co-hosts can kick off friendly head-to-head matchups, where viewers send chats, gifts, and Super Chats to push their creator’s score forward on-screen in real time,” YouTube Live product manager Barbara MacDonald wrote in a blog post .

Hopefully these impromptu collaborations with strangers won’t turn into a hotbed of bad behavior.

YouTube also shared data that provides insight into how people are using the platform. More people continue to watch YouTube on household TVs , and more than half of the top 100 YouTube creators have “living room” as their most watched interface.

YouTube’s data also confirms what we know about the growth of the microdrama industry : In the first half of 2026, microdramas on YouTube surpassed 6.5 billion views, and their watch time rose 50% year-over-year. People even seem to be watching these episodic, vertical video series on the big screen, with views of microdrama content on TVs increasing 90% year-over-year.

articles.title: YouTube’s new ‘Shorts series’ feature brings episodic viewing to Shorts
articles.summary: Other Made On YouTube announcements are also designed to help creators grow and engage audiences.
articles.body:
As microdrama apps gain traction , YouTube is clearly betting that episodic short-form storytelling will stick around. And that the format belongs on Shorts.

At its Made On YouTube event on Wednesday, the company announced “Shorts series,” a new tool that lets creators organize their Shorts into TV-style seasons and episodes. The feature brings a more traditional episodic structure to YouTube Shorts, complete with custom thumbnails and playback.

With Shorts series, viewers can watch a selection of Shorts as a continuous story rather than simply scrolling from one stand-alone clip to the next. The series will live on a creator’s YouTube channel.

The feature is rolling out to creators in the YouTube Partner Program across web, mobile, and connected TVs.

The move comes as no surprise, given that YouTubers have already been experimenting with microdramas and, increasingly, they’re considering it a serious business venture.

For instance, internet personality Hannah Stocking has crossed into vertical drama, starring in the musical microdrama “ Playback ,” which premiered on Holywater’s My Drama platform. Then there’s Joshua Ovenshire (The Jovenshire), a longtime YouTube creator who has moved away from traditional YouTube videos. He now works as an executive producer, making shows for vertical platform ReelShort, including a “Love Island”-inspired series called “ Secrets and Soulmates .”

The format has even become popular enough to attract recognizable Hollywood names , with celebrities including James Franco, Issa Rae, and Jesse Tyler Ferguson getting involved.

YouTube’s new feature also puts the platform more directly into competition with a growing collection of microdrama apps. TikTok recently launched PineDrama , its own microdrama app, while others such as ReelShort and DramaBox have also grown in popularity.

For YouTube, Shorts series could be a way to keep viewers engaged without sending them off to other platforms for episodic vertical storytelling. Instead, they’re providing a way to access it all directly on YouTube.

The company adds that Shorts series builds on “Creator Shows,” which it announced at its annual upfront event last year. This gave select creators the tools to organize their content into a viewing experience designed for TV. Creators, including Michelle Khare and Rhett & Link, used the tools to structure their content into seasons and episodes, making it easier for viewers to binge on the big screen.

Other Made On YouTube announcements are also designed to help creators grow and engage audiences. This includes “Live Showdowns,” which let creators pair up for interactive team challenges; expanded video A/B testing to compare different cuts or opening hooks; “Dynamic Thumbnails” to allow YouTubers to select the most engaging option from up to three creator-provided thumbnails for different audiences; new shopping features; and more.

articles.title: YouTube releases new AI features for creators within its Studio app | TechCrunch
articles.summary: YouTube is adding new features to generate ideas and monitor the performance of thumbnails.
articles.body:
At its Made On YouTube annual event, YouTube announced new tools for YouTube Studio, the app creators use to manage their channels, aimed at helping them analyze their videos and grow their audiences. The updates include expanding Ask Studio, its AI-powered Q&A feature, to iOS and Android, as well as new features that provide feedback on drafts and create dynamic thumbnails.

The draft-feedback feature uses AI to look at a creator’s unpublished video and provide suggestions about pacing, structure, and storytelling. YouTube is also debuting a new research feed in the Studio app that shows creators what kind of content is working on the platform, so they can apply their own take on it.

Creators are typically picky about the preview images and titles they use for their videos. The Studio app will now let them generate thumbnails and titles based on a video’s content and matched to their style. Creators can also use a new dynamic thumbnail feature to generate three options and show each one to a different segment of their audience.

YouTube said creators have used its A/B testing feature to run more than 40 million tests on titles and thumbnails. Soon, the company said, users will be able to test up to three video cuts to see which opening hook works best. Later this year, YouTube Studio will also automatically monitor thumbnail performance and change one proactively if it doesn’t perform well.

YouTube also said it’s updating its analytics to go beyond raw numbers, explaining why videos perform the way they do and providing advice about how to make content more engaging.

Besides the Studio app revamp, YouTube also introduced other tools for creators, including conversational editing in Shorts and the YouTube Create app.

articles.title: YouTube will let you build your own algorithm with AI | TechCrunch
articles.summary: YouTube’s new custom feeds let users describe the videos they want to see in their own words, then use Gemini to build a personalized feed around the request.
articles.body:
YouTube says it’s going to let you build your own algorithm — well, kind of. The company on Wednesday announced a new feature called custom feeds that allows you to describe, in your own words, the kinds of videos you’d like YouTube to recommend to you.

To create one, you type a description of what you want the feed to be about into a prompt box on YouTube, whether that’s a feed dedicated to a particular interest or one that serves some other purpose. For instance, YouTube suggests you could build a feed of video podcasts to watch during your 30-minute train commute, or you could request videos for a particular mood, like “relaxing commentary videos to unwind with.”

The prompt-based feature leverages Google’s Gemini AI model to build the feed around your request, and the resulting feed is then pinned to the top of your YouTube home page in its own tab. Because the feed’s creation is AI-powered, the request can be described in lengthy terms, as you share detailed information about how you want to curate the feed, what it should feature or exclude, what content to prioritize, and more.

The addition follows similar moves by a number of other social networks that have created tools that essentially allow users to build their own algorithms by describing what they want their feed to include and how to present that information to them.

Decentralized social network Bluesky began popularizing this idea years ago as a way to differentiate its service from rivals like X. This year, it rolled out an AI tool, Attie, that makes feed-building even easier. Other services, including Meta’s Threads , Instagram , X , and, more recently, Spotify , have also launched their own feed-building features, many of which are also AI-powered.

YouTube believes custom feeds will help users better explore the vast number of videos now hosted on its platform.

“One of the amazing things about being on YouTube is that the world is always at your fingertips,” noted Emily Moxley, VP of Product Management for Viewer AI, in a pre-brief with reporters ahead of the Made On YouTube event on Wednesday, where custom feeds were introduced to the public. “There’s over 20 billion videos in the YouTube corpus, so you’re always one search away from a treasure trove of topics.”

The new feeds, however, will not replace YouTube’s main feed, which features all your recommendations. Instead, you will now be able to easily hop right into whichever feed best suits your purposes when you open the YouTube app.

Support for creating multiple custom feeds will roll out across YouTube on web and mobile, starting next month, the company said.

articles.title: YouTube Music gets more conversational with new AI features | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Built directly into the YouTube Music app, Ask Music lets users describe what they want to hear in everyday language rather than searching for individual songs or artists.
articles.body:
YouTube is adding new AI-powered features to YouTube Music that aim to make it easier for listeners to discover music, explore artists, and find podcasts they may otherwise miss.

Announced at this year’s Made On YouTube event, the updates include “Ask Music,” a conversational tool for music and podcasts, and “Your Podcast Lineup,” a personalized audio guide designed to help listeners discover new shows.

Built directly into the YouTube Music app, Ask Music lets users describe what they want to hear in everyday language rather than searching for individual songs or artists. The feature works across YouTube Music’s catalog of more than 300 million songs, including official recordings, remixes, live performances, covers, and DJ sets. Users can use it to build custom listening queues, explore an artist’s motivations, or dig deeper into music history.

YouTube explains that, instead of manually searching, the user simply types the request as if they were asking a friend. For instance, someone could ask Ask Music to create a mix based on the tracks that inspired a particular song. Users can also ask other questions, such as who played bass on a particular song or other details about its creation.

YouTube Music is also introducing Your Podcast Lineup, a personalized AI-generated audio guide for podcast discovery.

The feature is designed for a familiar problem: There are more podcasts than most people have time to listen to. Even listeners who already have a list of favorite shows can struggle to keep up with new episodes, let alone find new ones.

Your Podcast Lineup will appear on the podcast page in the YouTube Music app. Each week, it will provide a short spoken preview of recommended shows and explain why they might appeal to the listener. It can then move directly into suggested episodes.

Spotify recently introduced an AI-powered feature that follows a similar direction. Its personal podcasts feature uses AI to generate podcast episodes based on their interests and prompts.

The new features are part of YouTube’s broader push to use AI throughout its services. Last year, YouTube Music experimented with AI-powered music hosts that provide stories, fan trivia, and commentary related to what users are listening to.

Both updates are coming soon to YouTube Music and YouTube Premium subscribers worldwide.

articles.title: YouTube's conversational video editing tool lets creators make edits in natural language | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Creators will be able to use AI in a conversational chat interface to help them edit videos.
articles.body:
YouTube announced a bunch of new creator tools at Wednesday’s Made On YouTube event, including a conversational editing tool that uses natural language to refine both long- and short-form footage.

“A one-hour shoot can be 10 hours or more in the edit. So, what if we could speed that process along without sacrificing any of our creative control?” YouTuber Happy Kelli shared onstage.

In a chat interface, creators give the AI instructions on how to help them put a video together. In Happy Kelli’s example, she shares footage of her dancing in different outfits and asks the AI to select the best take for each outfit. Then, she adds music and transitions that go along with the dance.

“If at any point I want even more control, I can jump back into the editing timeline and manually adjust things myself,” she said. “Overall, conversational editing turns the process of editing into a literal conversation with an infinitely patient helper. It’s a collaborative partner that edits with you, not for you.”

This feature can also add text overlays, remove pauses in speech, and more. It can also make suggestions to the creator based on the context of the conversation.

While some creators may find that this tool saves them time and speeds up the often tedious process of video editing, others may feel that their individual editing style sets their videos apart and be reluctant to relinquish control to an AI.

Conversational editing will be available for both YouTube Shorts and the YouTube Create app in early 2027.

articles.title: YouTube is making comments more fun — and fandom more lucrative for creators | TechCrunch
articles.summary: YouTube is rolling out GIF replies, voice-powered TV comments, personalized moderation, paid members-only communities, and new ways for fans to support their favorite creators.
articles.body:
YouTube’s comments section is getting an upgrade, alongside the rollout of other community-focused features such as exclusive paid memberships, the company announced at its Made On YouTube event on Wednesday. Commenters will now be able to respond with GIFs or leave comments from their TVs, while creators will get new tools to support their fan communities, including features to personalize moderation, invite members into VIP-like areas, and give fans new ways to help them make money from their content.

Comments are still one of the main ways YouTube viewers interact with creators’ content, but they’ve often lagged behind other social networks’ commenting features. For instance, TikTok just announced that commenters can respond to videos with their voice and add polls, photo carousels, and Live Photos to their comments. Spotify lets video podcasters use polls and Q&As to engage their audiences.

YouTube is finally catching up a bit by adding support for leaving GIFs in comments and letting users comment while watching YouTube on TV. The latter works by voice, not painfully typing out “LOL” on your remote control, YouTube noted.

One of the more interesting additions is a new comment moderation tool that’s personalized to each creator’s needs. Though YouTube already offers a comment moderation filter, creators may want to tailor it more precisely, particularly on live videos, where it’s harder to keep up. For now, the company is calling this personalized moderation an “experiment” and didn’t provide specific technical details about how it works.

Other features are meant to help creators grow their fan communities — and make money from that fandom. These arrive at a time when revenue from advertising is no longer the only way creators monetize their videos.

The company said its Channel Memberships features are evolving, with the addition of paid, members-only communities, where members can share posts and start discussions with other top fans. YouTube will market these communities alongside other memberships on a new “channel memberships” page for viewers, designed to help them discover ones that match their interests.

Hype , a feature that lets fans recommend smaller creators’ videos to others and climb fan leaderboards, will gain new functionality dubbed “Hype with Jewels.” Previously, fans could only “hype” videos three times per week for free. Now they can buy Jewels, a virtual currency of sorts, to hype videos even more, helping to support creators and grow their audience. Fans motivated by clout may also appreciate that their handles will be permanently added to the video’s description.

YouTube said viewers have so far hyped more than 75 million unique videos over 1 billion times.

The company’s direct messaging feature for sharing videos with family and friends will also support group chats in the next few months. Users will be able to record quick, raw videos and share them in these conversations, too.

These community-focused features arrived alongside other creator tools, including those for A/B testing, live dubbing , AI-assisted video editing, and more.

articles.title: Exclusive: Zoox grounds Atlanta test fleet after workers report toxic gas exposure symptoms
articles.summary: The repeated incidents led one worker to file a complaint with the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, which opened an inquiry and told Zoox to investigate the exposures.
articles.body:
Zoox has grounded its autonomous vehicle test fleet in Atlanta after safety drivers were potentially exposed to carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, or hydrogen sulfide gas inside its vehicles last month, TechCrunch has learned. The repeated incidents led one worker to file a complaint with the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, which opened an inquiry and told Zoox to investigate the exposures.

As many as 40 workers were possibly exposed to the gases in the vehicles, according to a letter from OSHA to Zoox that TechCrunch viewed, though the Amazon-owned company says the number is lower.

Zoox put at least one group of workers back on the road in a different car after one vomited and the rest reported exposure symptoms, a contractor told TechCrunch. That second car may have also contained potentially toxic gases, he said, because the workers experienced another bout of exposure symptoms later that day.

“They made us go right back in the field after we said we were throwing up,” Jay Davis, one of the contractors who got sick in mid-August, told TechCrunch in an interview. “I emailed HR, told her what’s going on, and I told her I feel like it’s messed up that y’all made us go [back out].”

Workers reported exposure symptoms and strange smells through much of last month until August 22, when someone called 911 for a sick worker. The facility in northwest Atlanta has operated at limited capacity since then, with the test vehicles quarantined while Zoox investigated the exposures, according to two employees. Zoox’s purpose-built robotaxis, which are all electric, are not affected.

TechCrunch spoke to Davis, who filed the OSHA complaint, along with one current and two former employees for this story. The other three workers were granted anonymity to discuss private company matters and because they fear retaliation.

The illnesses come as Zoox branches into new cities and expands its existing operations in places like Las Vegas and San Francisco, in a bid to catch market leader Waymo. This rapid growth has put some safety monitors at risk. As TechCrunch previously reported , contractors have sustained injuries from sudden braking and swerving in the Zoox test vehicles. Waymo has also reported similar test driver injuries to OSHA.

Exactly what gases the Zoox employees were exposed to remains unclear. Davis said he and two other workers who became sick were told at the emergency room that their symptoms were consistent with carbon monoxide exposure. The complaint filed with OSHA mentions possible carbon dioxide, or CO 2 , exposure.

Zoox told OSHA in a September 10 letter, viewed by TechCrunch, that it examined its test vehicles for signs of CO 2 and replaced their 12-volt batteries. Damaged batteries can produce hydrogen sulfide gas, which creates a “rotten egg” smell. Some of the employees who spoke to TechCrunch said they noticed a similar smell in the cars.

Zoox identified 28 employees who rode in six test vehicles that had an “unexplained odor,” the company said in its letter to OSHA. Zoox told OSHA that 10 workers “voluntarily underwent medical evaluation” to “determine whether any exposure had occurred.” Zoox said in the letter that it received only “one medical report identifying CO 2 exposure.”

Zoox told TechCrunch it hasn’t identified the presence of carbon monoxide, which is odorless, in its vehicles. The company said it consulted an outside medical expert to help investigate the issues and that the only gas it detected in the impacted vehicles was CO 2 .

In the letter to OSHA, the company said it will add CO 2 monitors to the vehicles. OSHA has since closed its inquiry.

“The safety and well-being of our Zoox test fleet operators is our primary concern in this situation,” the company told TechCrunch. “We are taking ongoing, appropriate, and cautious actions to investigate the reported events as necessary and support any needs from our operators. While we investigate these reports thoroughly, we have ceased operations of our test vehicles in this market.”

Cars produce carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide when they burn fuel. These gases can enter a vehicle if there is a leak in the exhaust system; they can also build up if a vehicle runs inside an enclosed space for an extended period. It’s a common enough problem that the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration investigated Ford for six years over reports of carbon monoxide buildup in its Explorer SUVs.

In its letter to OSHA, Zoox said it tested the vehicles’ exhaust systems for leaks and performed a “smoke test” for cabin intrusions. It did not say whether it found any evidence of either. The company also removed all the 12-volt batteries, inspected them for damage, and replaced them. It did not tell OSHA whether it found evidence of damage to the batteries.

The company keeps its test vehicles running through much of a given day, in part to maintain sensor calibration and reduce the onboard self-driving computer’s boot time. Zoox uses an exhaust-capture system at its indoor depots — similar to what is used to capture truck fumes at firehouses — designed to mitigate the buildup of toxic gases.

Zoox modifies the Highlander SUVs it uses for its test fleet. Most of that work focuses on adding sensors and an autonomy computer. But the company makes other changes, too, including adding an interior “snorkel” above the central infotainment screen that pushes air toward rear-seat passengers, the employees told TechCrunch.

Zoox said it doesn’t modify the ventilation systems in these SUVs. But making any changes to a vehicle can increase the risk that gases will leak into the cabin. In the Ford investigation, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said in 2023 that the highest levels of carbon monoxide were found in police vehicles that had added sirens, lights, and other modifications, all of which can create sealing issues.

Zoox is an outlier among major robotaxi developers because its test fleet vehicles have internal combustion engines. Waymo, Tesla, Avride, and Motional all use electric vehicles, which don’t produce exhaust gases. May Mobility’s test fleet includes some hybrid vans, and Nvidia uses a small number of gas and electric Mercedes-Benz sedans.

Davis and the other employees said individual safety monitors started reporting possible exposure symptoms to Zoox at the beginning of August.

The incidents Davis experienced on August 14 were more acute because four workers were riding in the SUVs together — a practice Zoox uses while training new employees.

Davis told TechCrunch the first signs of trouble appeared early that morning.

“Everything was fine. We was all laughing and talking, you know, just having a normal workday, and then everybody got quiet for some reason,” he said.

Davis recalled that one of his colleagues asked if anyone else in the SUV was “feeling weird.” The crew was approaching their scheduled morning break at 10 a.m., so the workers stopped at a Chick-fil-A. As soon as they got out of the car, Davis said one of his co-workers started throwing up. He and the others felt lightheaded.

They called the dispatcher at Zoox’s Atlanta depot, who arranged for the SUV to be towed back to base, he said. Meanwhile, Zoox arranged for an Uber to take the workers back to the depot.

“As soon as we get back to base, we’re thinking, okay, since we’ve been sick and said we was lightheaded, you know, we’re gonna have like, you know, mild duties for the day. Just sit down, you know, get yourself back together,” Davis said. “No, they put us in another [test car] and they told us to go back to work.”

After driving all afternoon, Davis said he and his colleagues went to a food court. He started vomiting after just a few bites of his meal.

Davis contacted a representative from HireArt, the third-party contractor that technically employs Zoox’s test drivers in Atlanta. He said the representative gave him a workers’ compensation hotline number and told him to call Poison Control. Three of the workers went to the emergency room, where they were evaluated for carbon monoxide exposure.

Davis said the emergency room doctor did not detect elevated carbon monoxide levels in his system. But he and others were told their symptoms were consistent with carbon monoxide poisoning.

Workers continued getting sick in the days that followed, according to all four workers who spoke to TechCrunch. On August 22, one contractor got sick enough that someone at the depot called 911.

It’s not immediately clear who called 911 or what happened to the sick worker. As for the four employees who reported symptoms on August 14, Zoox ordered them to take what it described as a random drug test in the days that followed.

articles.title: Modal Motors is trying to cut China out of electric motors entirely | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The startup is working on small, light motors with no rare-earth magnets that are suited for drones, fans, and robots.
articles.body:
Lately, it seems like everyone is talking about bringing manufacturing back to the United States, especially when it comes to hard tech like drones and robotics. Michael Van Steenburg thinks he’s ahead of the game.

Van Steenburg spent the last decade building all kinds of electric motors in the U.S. and North America, and now he wants to do it again with his new startup, Modal Motors . This time, he wants to ditch rare-earth magnets entirely, in a bid to further separate the U.S. from China’s supply chain.

As one of the founders in Startup Battlefield 200 who will compete at TechCrunch Disrupt next month, he thinks it’s an urgent pitch to make.

“China’s already flexed its muscles a couple times,” Van Steenburg said, referring to the country restricting access to rare-earth products .

There are other companies working on setting up electric motor manufacturing and supply chains in the U.S., but Van Steenburg argues they’re doing it the wrong way by continuing to rely on rare-earth magnets. Domestic supply of those materials is still years away, he said.

“Other people are ‘reshoring,’ [but] they’re basically knocking off Chinese motors and just doing it in the U.S. But they’re hoping that the U.S. rare-earth magnet system is going to get up to speed fast enough,” he said. “It’s going to still be a while longer before they can actually replace China.”

Modal Motors has two products that it’s developing ahead of Disrupt. One is a small electric motor meant for drones that can also work in fans, blowers, and even actuators. It’s designed to “minimize mass while delivering maximum torque density and efficiency,” according to the startup’s website.

The more radical design is what Modal refers to as the “Hybrid Enigma Drive,” a planar — or flat — electric motor that can fit in lower-profile spaces.

Van Steenburg is drawing on decades of experience in the automotive industry to develop these motors and get them customer-ready. But there’s also an irony in the work Van Steenburg is doing to make Modal Motors’ products a China-free option; in the late 1990s, he worked on a hybrid gas-electric drivetrain that China wanted to put in its so-called “People’s Car.”

“It’s kind of comical,” he said, thinking back on that experience and how much the world has changed. What hasn’t changed, he said, is his outsider streak and strong conviction about doing things that are hard.

“I always tell people that the clock started ticking 25 years ago, and in that whole time, I’ve watched a slow-motion train wreck as China’s been going around the world, grabbing mines, grabbing mineral rights, doing all these things, and slowly but surely monopolizing the entire rare-earth supply chain,” he said.

articles.title: Enveda secures $311M to bring more nature-derived AI drugs into clinical trials | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The round valued the AI biotech at $2 billion. It is currently testing drugs that treat skin conditions and preserve weight loss after stopping GLP-1s.
articles.body:
Enveda , a biotech startup that uses AI to discover new drugs in the natural world, has raised a $311 million Series E at a $2 billion valuation. The fresh funding, which was led by Catalio Capital Management, with participation from Iconiq and others, doubles the valuation Enveda achieved 12 months ago.

The idea behind Enveda is that powerful medicines could be harnessed from plants and microbes, rather than synthesized from scratch in a lab. Viswa Colluru, an early employee of Recursion Pharmaceuticals, founded Enveda in 2019 to speed up the process of discovering these new drugs using AI and other techniques.

While AI hasn’t yet produced any FDA-approved drugs, Enveda is among the wave of companies advancing AI-discovered candidates into human clinical trials. The startup is currently testing several drugs in patients, including one targeting severe skin conditions and another designed to help maintain weight loss after stopping GLP-1s.

articles.title: VC firm Bessemer now has another $5.75B to invest in (what else?) AI | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The VC firm says that AI-native companies are growing faster than any technology, ever.
articles.body:
Bessemer Venture Partners announced on Wednesday that it has raised $5.75 billion across two new funds to accelerate its investment across all parts of the AI stack. The firm, which has backed companies such as Anthropic, Cognition, Legora, Perplexity, Ramp, Shopify, and Waymo, dedicated $1.75 billion for seed and early-stage investing and the remaining $4 billion for growth startups.

Bessemer has been well-known as a leading VC in the SaaS era , with a particular knack for picking enterprise winners, like Box, Docusign, and Gainsight. Since 2022, it has invested in more than 260 AI-native companies. So far, the firm has invested $3 billion into AI-related startups, it says, including those focused on compute, infrastructure, foundation models, dev tools, app-layer startups, and agentic tech.

Now, Bessemer positions all things AI as the opportunity of a lifetime — a common sentiment, until the next big trendy tech revolution comes around, of course.

“AI-native companies are scaling faster than any category of technology we’ve backed before,” Bessemer Partner Byron Deeter said in the company’s funding announcement. VC firms also need to keep increasing their war chests, Deeter told Bloomberg , because companies staying private longer has become “a permanent structural shift.”

articles.title: Vogue sent robots down the runway at Vogue World, and people were not impressed | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Nothing says Italian craftsmanship like a Chinese robot doing a lasso to "L'Amour Toujours."
articles.body:
Vogue World closed its Milan edition this week with a troupe of robots — perhaps a preview of what’s coming when the event descends on San Francisco next year.

Vogue World is the magazine’s annual traveling spectacle, now in its fifth year: part runway show, part celebrity showcase, part variety hour, part ad-sales opportunity , staged in a different city each time. It has run through New York, London, Paris, and Hollywood. This year’s Milan edition was marketed as a tribute to Italian craftsmanship and “the human touch” in an age of technology, which makes what happened next a little strange.

During the act titled The Age of Intelligence, humanoid robots made by the Chinese firm Unitree walked into the Galleria to Gigi D’Agostino’s “L’Amour Toujours.” They waved their arms in the air, imploring onlookers to clap. One did a lasso. They were not wearing clothes. The pained expression of Alessandro Michele, the creative director of Valentino, quickly went viral.

I haven’t seen a single thing about the actual fashion that was presented at Vogue World Milan. Instead, everyone is talking about the robots. (These same robots have been making headlines worldwide for their dance moves , and for falling and breaking .) Similar robots turned up on the runway at London Fashion Week, which is happening now.

Vogue turned heads earlier this year when it announced that the next edition will be in San Francisco, arguably one of the least stylish cities in the United States. The timing isn’t coincidental. Anna Wintour has aligned herself ever more closely with the tech barons of our time, and Vogue World Milan was itself sponsored in part by Meta Glasses, with additional support from OpenAI.

It was one of those moments that reveals how thoroughly tech exists in a bubble, and that not everyone is happy with the rapid adoption of new technology, or by Vogue cozying up to the symbols of the insanely rich — and only getting richer — tech titans during a cost-of-living crisis. That’s before you get to AI, mass surveillance, the displacement of labor, and the energy crisis, all of them overseen by the same titans. For some, a robot on a runway is further proof of what is going wrong in the world right now.

“I’m annoyed by the celebrities cheering the whole thing,” one tech founder wrote me on Instagram. “It’s sick and gloom. People are literally losing jobs and livelihoods because of these things. They need to stop encouraging it. What’s it even modeling? Headphones?”

One fashion reporter friend simply said “No,” when I asked for thoughts on the robots and Vogue World San Francisco. Jason Johnson, founder of Culture Impact Agency, noted that Vogue has been trying to build a relationship with Silicon Valley for at least the past decade, highlighting when Jony Ive co-hosted the Met Gala back in 2015. The dancing robots at Vogue World Milan were inevitable, then, as is Vogue World San Francisco and as was Jeff Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sanchez, getting the splashy Vogue wedding cover and co-hosting the 2026 Met Gala.

“Publications are figuring out new ways to make money and tech has money,” he told me. “Vogue has the cultural influence and access that those tech people want.” Both sides win in the end, he said.

Still, something about the way Vogue is going about this feels unnatural.

Muna Ikedionwu, founder of MKEDI, a strategy firm for early-stage startups, said what she found most interesting about the robots is that they don’t fully represent the innovation and progress that’s actually happening in the creative technologist space. “I’ve seen such incredible examples of engineering and AI being used to influence fashion, being used to influence design and art,” she told me, adding that robots walking down the runway doesn’t even scratch the surface of what is happening right now at the intersection of fashion and tech.

She points to the artist duo AA Murakami , who created Olympian Eileen Gu’s dress of bubbles at this year’s Met Gala . They are fashion designers but also engineers, Ikedionwu said, noting a presentation she saw them give recently about how to create an “everlasting bubble.” They are helping to pioneer “emphemeral technology,” she said, “this idea of technology and innovation that speaks to the ephemeral nature or the temporariness of art and humanity and the soul.”

Sure, I guess when you compare it to this, the robots did seem quite boring. Whenever I think about the intersection of fashion and technology, I think about that Spring 2024 Schiaparelli collection , which unveiled a robot baby crafted with Swarovski crystals and a dress made with vintage tech like PC microchips. (I once threatened to wear that dress to Disrupt; see image above.)

Ikedionwu wonders whether this robot performance was a way to make the general public more comfortable with technology and fashion overlapping, a merger that has been underway behind the scenes for years. If so, it didn’t work. But maybe Vogue World is saving all the good stuff for San Francisco.
